performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; Kosti Vehanen, piano
intro: Marian Anderson recorded Florence Price’s arrangement of this spiritual for Victor in New York on 4 February 1936, with Kosti Vehanen at the piano. Victor issued the disc in February 1937, on a ten-inch Red Seal record that also carried Harry T. Burleigh’s Go Down, Moses.

sections.label: A · Opening, “In the Lord, in the Lord”

cues.title: Refrain and two couplets
cues.text: The words are a refrain, “In the Lord, in the Lord, my soul’s been anchored in the Lord”, and two couplets: “Before I’d stay in hell one day / I’d sing and pray myself away” and “I’m going to pray and never stop / Until I’ve reached the mountain top”.
cues.evidence: Text as printed by Song of America, which lists the Hildegard Publishing edition (ed. Vivian Taylor, Art Songs and Spirituals by African-American Women Composers) as the sheet music for the song: https://songofamerica.net/song/my-souls-been-anchored-in-the-lord . The 1937 Remick and Gamble editions were not seen.

cues.title: Manuscript of 1931, edition of 1937
cues.text: Price’s manuscript of the arrangement is dated 30 September 1931 and dedicated to Abbie Mitchell. Gamble Hinged Music Co. registered it for copyright on 12 August 1937, six months after the record appeared. The Remick edition of 1937 is marked “As sung by Marian Anderson (Victor Record No. 1799)”.
cues.evidence: Florence B. Price Works Catalog, “My Soul’s Been Anchored in the Lord”: composition year 1931; complete manuscript dated 30 September 1931 (University of Arkansas, MC988b, Box 1C, Folder 35) with the annotation “Arr. especially for and dedicated to Abbie Mitchell”; copyright 12 August 1937, Gamble Hinged Music Co., E pub. 63815; Remick Music edition, 1937, annotated “As sung by Marian Anderson (Victor Record No. 1799)”: https://fbpricecatalog.net/price-my-souls-been-anchored/ . Record release February 1937: Discography of American Historical Recordings, Victor 1799, https://adp.library.ucsb.edu/index.php/objects/detail/12544

cues.title: A reviewer on the piano part, 1937
cues.text: In February 1937 The American Record Guide reviewed the disc. A. P. D. thought the arrangement “overdone in the elaborate piano accompaniment” and in a “theatrical ending”, and wrote that Vehanen “catches the syncopation of the piano part” and plays brilliantly.
cues.evidence: The American Record Guide, vol. 2 no. 10 (February 1937), record reviews, “Spirituals: Go Down Moses, and My Soul’s Been Anchored in the Lord”, 10-inch Victor 1799, signed A. P. D.: https://archive.org/details/sim_american-record-guide_1937-02_2_10

cues.title: Lincoln Memorial, 9 April 1939
cues.text: Anderson sang the arrangement at the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday 1939, with Vehanen at the piano. The printed programme listed it last of three spirituals, after Burleigh’s Gospel Train and Boatner’s Trampin’. Some 75,000 people attended, and six microphones served the crowd and the radio broadcast.
cues.evidence: Cait Miller, “Marian Anderson’s #LincolnMemorialMoment”, Library of Congress, In The Muse, 12 May 2022, citing the printed programme in the Coolidge Foundation Collection (Box 2/Folder 30): the set list ends with three spirituals, “Gospel Train” (Burleigh), “Trampin’” (Boatner) and Price’s adaptation, with Kosti Vehanen at the piano: https://blogs.loc.gov/music/2022/05/marian-andersons-lincoln-memorial-moment/

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings lists Anderson as vocalist (contralto) and Vehanen as pianist, and describes the matrix as a contralto vocal solo with piano. The Internet Archive creator field lists Price, Anderson and Vehanen.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Price’s arrangement for voice and piano, as sung by Marian Anderson on Victor 1799. The disc label gives the title as “My Soul’s Been Anchored in the Lord”.
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings names Florence Price as arranger, from the disc label, and the Remick edition of 1937 is annotated “As sung by Marian Anderson (Victor Record No. 1799)”. Which printed or manuscript version the singer and pianist used (key, cuts, ending) is not stated, and neither the Remick nor the Gamble edition was seen. The Internet Archive file is titled “My Souls Been Anchored In The Lord”.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Matrix BS-99538 was recorded on 4 February 1936; takes 1, 1A, 2 and 2A are listed for that day and take 2 is the master issued on Victor 1799 and Gramophone DA-1560. The Internet Archive date of 1937 is the year of release, not of the session.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: As given for every take of the matrix in the Discography of American Historical Recordings.

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Victor (Camden, N.J.), 10-inch double-faced Red Seal; the same take was issued as Gramophone DA-1560
fields.note: The Discography of American Historical Recordings describes Victor 1799 as a 10-inch double-faced Red Seal and lists the same two matrices under Gramophone DA-1560. The Internet Archive item gives the publisher as Victor.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Victor 1799, side B (coupled with Burleigh’s “Go Down, Moses”, matrix BS-99537); released February 1937
fields.note: Release date 2/1937 is given by the Discography of American Historical Recordings from the Victor catalog. The American Record Guide reviewed the disc in February 1937 at $1.50. The Internet Archive item records the side as “1799-B”, which is the label side designation; its “Matrix number: 1799B” is not a Victor matrix number.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: Take 2 is the master issued on Victor 1799 and on Gramophone DA-1560. That the Internet Archive transfer is of the Victor 1799 pressing rests on the item’s description (“Victor (1799-B)”).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Digitised by George Blood, L.P. for the Internet Archive’s Great 78 Project
fields.note: The item metadata gives George Blood, L.P. as the scanning centre and the item belongs to the collections 78rpm, georgeblood, archiveofcontemporarymusic and audio_music.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Internet Archive lists the item as added on 11 February 2017; that is the upload, not the date of the transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Four styli (2.0, 2.3, 2.8 and 3.3 mil truncated conical) were used; the transfers were made flat and also equalised with a turnover of 500. The preferred version is the equalised transfer with the 2.3 mil stylus, copied as the file used here (named “restored”).
fields.note: From the item description. Noise reduction and any speed correction are not described.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Price died on 3 June 1953, so her arrangement has been out of copyright in the EU and the United Kingdom (life plus 70 years) since 1 January 2024. In the United States it was registered for copyright on 12 August 1937 by Gamble Hinged Music Co.; whether that copyright was renewed was not checked. The underlying spiritual is traditional.
fields.note: The registration is documented by the Price Works Catalog. The EU term is a calculation from her death date, which the composer chapter on this site gives. Rights in the composition are separate from rights in the recording and do not block publication.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Territorial EU public domain: first published before 1963 (Victor 1799, released February 1937). United States status not established: a recording first published in 1937 is still within the term of federal protection for pre-1972 recordings, and the Internet Archive item sits in the collection that was the subject of UMG Recordings, Inc. v. Internet Archive.
fields.note: The release date comes from the Victor catalog as given by the Discography of American Historical Recordings, and a review of the disc appeared in February 1937. For recordings first published between 1923 and 1946 the Copyright Office describes a term of 95 years plus 5 years after first publication, which for 1937 runs to the end of 2037. The Great 78 Project was the subject of a lawsuit by record companies, settled confidentially in September 2025 (reported by Music Business Worldwide, and acknowledged by the Internet Archive on 15 September 2025); its terms were not published. The item’s curation note of 22 August 2025 reads “lawsuit temporary undark and noindex”: the item was restored to view but is withheld from search indexing. On 19 October 2026 the Internet Archive record of the British pressing of the same take (HMV DA 1560, item 78_my-souls-been-anchored-in-the-lord_marian-anderson-kosti-vehanen-price_gbia0125732b) was marked dark. If the Internet Archive withdraws this item, the stream will fail.

composer.epithet: American composer whose symphonic music used the juba dance and the brass hymn as central elements.
facts: New England Conservatory, 1903–06; diplomas in organ performance and piano teaching
Teacher in Arkansas and Atlanta; pianist, organist and composer in Chicago from 1927
Symphonies, concertos, chamber music, piano and organ pieces, songs and spiritual arrangements

quote.text: I should like to be judged on merit alone.

composer.background:
On 15 June 1933 Florence Price came onto the stage of Chicago’s Auditorium Theatre in a long white gown. Frederick Stock and the Chicago Symphony Orchestra had just played her Symphony No. 1 in E minor, and the applause kept bringing her back. It was the first time a major American orchestra had performed a symphony by a Black woman. Maude Roberts George, president of the Chicago Music Association and a critic for the Chicago Defender, had raised money to underwrite the concert. The performance was part of the city’s Century of Progress celebrations. Price was forty-six.

She was born Florence Beatrice Smith in Little Rock on 9 April 1887. Her father, James, was a dentist; her mother taught her the piano. She had her first musical education at home, and she was publishing pieces while still at school. In 1903 she went to the New England Conservatory in Boston. At its 1906 commencement concert she played the first movement of Henry Dunham’s Organ Sonata in G minor. The programme names her Florence Beatrice Smith.
